What I want is a strip of three sprites under the big one: small, medium, huge, with a little arrow between them and the level it happens at. Tap one, jump to it.

This is the one bit of Pokémon knowledge that is entirely pictures. Art cannot read CHARMELEON, but he can absolutely see that the small orange one turns into the big red one turns into the enormous winged one, and that is the whole idea of evolution delivered without a single word. For Gabe it's the thing he'd otherwise go and look up on a phone. Grey out the ones he hasn't caught and it doubles as a to-do list — three empty silhouettes he wants to fill in.

title: Champion's circuit says 58/58 and offers nothing
body:
I opened the Gym Circuit on the champion save (E-0067, and again at E-0096 after a whole session of fighting). There is exactly one number on it: TRAINERS DEFEATED 58/58, in grey. The headline card is CROWN ELITE FOUR + CHAMPION with all five progress boxes filled solid green — and the crossed swords "go fight this" icon still sitting on the right of a fight he finished weeks ago. Under it, twelve badges, all ticked. Under that, a heal button and a versus button. That's the whole endgame screen.

Per your own changelog, ROUND 2 is the entire point of this save state: 58 trainers back at +15 levels, Hiker Carl at Lv23, a MASTER BADGE at the end. On screen it is a chip at the top that is filled gold while ROUND 1 sits on plain cream paper — so the tab that looks pressed is the one you are not on, nothing beneath it has changed, and the counter reads 58/58 instead of 0/58. Walking into Boulder from here still gives Lv 8 Carl (E-0068).

Make ROUND 2 the hero card, with its own counter and its own empty boxes.

title: Endurance HP is invisible; healing is one grey line
body:
HP carrying from trainer to trainer inside a stop is a great idea. The problem is you can't see it anywhere.

On the Boulder Gym page (E-0068, E-0105) there is no HP at all: a header reading "5/5 DEFEATED — WIN TO CATCH THEIR TEAM!", then five trainer cards. No team strip, no bars, and no Poke Center button — the heal lives one screen back on the circuit (E-0096), so to check on his team mid-stop Gabe has to leave the stop.

Then the payoff. I pressed the big pink POKE CENTER — HEAL TEAM, and the entire response was one line of small pink text at the very bottom of the page, below the versus button: "YOUR TEAM IS FULLY HEALED!" That line is literally the only pixel difference between E-0096 and E-0097. Nothing moved, nothing flashed, no team shown, no bars refilling.

So he can't tell whether he needed healing, and after a rough fight he can't tell whether he's about to walk into Leader Rocko at 12 HP. Put a six-slot HP strip at the top of the stop page with the heal button beside it, and let the bars visibly refill.

title: Every rematch is a Lv8 fight labelled HALF XP
body:
On the champion save, Boulder Gym is five identical green cards, each carrying 🔁 REMATCH — HALF XP (E-0068, E-0105). "HALF XP" is the single most repeated string on the page — five times down one screen. The trainers behind those buttons are Lv 8, 9, 10, 11 and 13. The Charizard that walks in is Lv 62 (E-0069): a level sixty-two dragon against a one-Pokemon level eight Geodude, for half of almost nothing.

Two separate problems. First, the button leads with the deduction instead of the prize — the actual reason to rematch ("WIN TO CATCH THEIR TEAM") is printed once, in small type, in the header. A seven-year-old reads five green buttons that all say his reward is halved. Second, there is no route from this screen to a version of these same five trainers that would still be a fight.

Label the button with what he wins — 🔁 REMATCH → CATCH THEIR TEAM — and if a harder tier of this stop exists, put a gold "HIKER CARL Lv 23 — FULL XP" card right beside the Lv 8 one. (Adjacent to F-008, which is about the ceremony after the win. This is about the offer before it.)
rule_risk: never take something away from a child: the only label on a returning player's button is a halved reward

title: The stop roster shows exactly what you're walking into
body:
Boulder Gym's trainer list is the best-designed screen in my slice, and it renders identically on the mid and champion saves (E-0150, E-0068).

Five cards, top to bottom. A big portrait of the lead Pokemon. Then the trainer's actual team sprites, in the number they actually field — Carl one, Sandy two, Ruin Maniac Leo two, Leader Rocko three. A name. A one-line taunt in the trainer's own voice ("My fossils are old. My skills are TIMELESS."). And a level in the corner climbing 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, with LEADER ROCKO last.

Gabe can read the whole stop before he commits a single turn: how many fights, how many Pokemon each, how steep the ladder. And it tells the truth — I tapped the first card and got exactly the Geodude Lv 8 the card had drawn (E-0069).

Please keep this contract when Round 2 lands: sprites on the card = the real team, corner level = the real level, leader last. Worth a smoke check that the first trainer card's printed level equals the level of the Pokemon that actually appears in the battle.

title: A gauntlet: five trainers, one health bar
body:
The circuit already owns every part a tournament needs and never holds one. HP carries between trainers inside a stop. The stops are five-trainer ladders that already escalate. Badges already hang on a wall.

So: once a stop is cleared, put a GAUNTLET card on it. All five trainers back to back. No Poke Center in between. The six you started with are the six you finish with. Clear it and a ribbon lights up next to that stop's badge.

That is real difficulty without inventing a single new trainer or raising a single level, and it makes a Lv 8–13 roster mean something again to a Lv 62 team — which is exactly the problem on the champion's Boulder page today.

It is also rules-safe: he opts in, and if he falls over at trainer four nothing is taken from him. He keeps the badge, keeps the Pokemon, and the ribbon is simply not lit yet.

Right now the champion's circuit ends at a heal button (E-0096). This gives him something to press — and gives the ROUND 2 tab a second thing to be about.

title: Tapping a box Pokemon throws you out of the box
body:
Gabe has 620 caught. I opened his PC (E-0110), scrolled, and tapped Charmander at #004. The PC did not open a detail card — it slammed shut and dumped me on the main dex screen (E-0111). Same thing again mid-session: tapped one box Pokemon, ejected to dex; tapped another, ejected again (E-0139, E-0140).

Two things go wrong at 620. First, my place is gone. Reopening PC puts me back at the top of G1, so any tap costs me the whole scroll again — and in a 620 box that scroll was the expensive part. Second, it shows me the wrong Pokemon. The one I tapped is Gabe's SHINY Charmander at Lv 55; the dex page shows the ordinary species entry, SHINY button unpressed, no level, no nickname (E-0111). I asked about MY Charmander and got the encyclopedia article.

Art's box does the right thing here — his tap opens a little card in place, box still behind it (E-0031). Gabe's box should do that too: open, close, and I am still exactly where I was.

title: The ALL tab hangs half off the right edge
body:
The generation tabs across Gabe's box are the only way to cut 620 Pokemon down to something walkable, and on a 390-wide phone the strip does not fit. Open the PC cold and the leftmost tab is already sliced — you can read "1 5 1" but the label above it is chopped by the screen edge — while on the right, the ALL tab is reduced to a lone "A" and "6 2 0" falling off the edge (E-0110, and identical in E-0146).

There is no arrow, no fade, no half-peeking next tab that says "keep swiping." It just ends. The tab I most want as a hoarder — the one holding all 620 — is the one that is barely there, and the tab I am currently standing on is clipped too, so I cannot tell it is selected without squinting at the brighter green fill.

This is a small fix with a big payoff: shrink the tabs so all six fit, or put a visible chevron at each end. Right now the strip looks finished when it isn't.

title: Art sees nine Pokemon at a time out of 620
body:
I opened Art's box on the small phone with 620 caught (E-0030). Measuring the screenshot: the favourites shelf, the team strip and the tab row eat the top 242 of 667 pixels before a single box Pokemon appears, and the fat green BACK bar takes the bottom 90. What is left shows three full rows of three, plus a sliver — call it nine or ten Pokemon on screen at once.

Nine out of 620. That is roughly 65 screenfuls of flicking. Gabe at least has a search box; Art cannot type, so scroll is his only tool, and the gen tabs are his only filter. If he wants the Snorlax he caught on Tuesday and it isn't in his team strip, he is not going to find it. He will give up, and a 4-year-old giving up on his own collection is the outcome this whole screen exists to prevent.

The cards are lovely and the right size — I would not shrink them. I would give him a shorter header and something better than scrolling (see my wish). Confirmed unchanged after heavy mashing (E-0036).

title: Both brothers get the same six-slot team, lead marked without words
body:
This is the one part of the collection UI that scales cleanly and I want it nailed down before someone refactors it.

Gabe's box (E-0110) and Art's box (E-0030) show the exact same object: six slots, same order, same sprites, lead in position one. Gabe's lead has a gold border and a star; Art's lead has a gold-tinted cell and a small gold mark. Neither needs the word LEAD to know which one goes first — it is colour and position, which is precisely the rule CLAUDE.md sets out. Art can point at his Charizard and know it's the one that comes out first, and it is the same picture his big brother sees.

It also holds up on the small phone. All six of Art's slots fit on one row at 375 with nothing clipped (E-0030, E-0036) — worth pinning as a regression test, because other reviewers found the normal-mode strip losing a slot at that width.

One caveat while you're in there: Art's gold tint is tan-on-cream and much quieter than Gabe's gold border. Push it a shade.

title: Let me shelve by newest and by sparkle, not just by region
body:
Gabe's trainer card says CAUGHT 620 and SHINIES 12 (E-0145). Twelve. Those twelve are the twelve he is proudest of, and there is no way on earth to reach them except scrolling 620 cards looking for a gold sparkle. In this save they happen to sit at #001-#012 so the box looks sparkly at the top (E-0110); after the next shiny at #430 that stops being true.

Same problem with the newest catch. Catch something and it files itself into dex order, so the thing you just did lands at row 143 and vanishes. The moment of pride has nowhere to go.

I would add a small row of picture chips beside the gen tabs: a Poke Ball for NEWEST, a sparkle for SHINY, a star for FAVES. Icons only, so they work identically in Art's box — he cannot read G1 either, and a sparkle chip that fills his screen with just the special ones is the single best thing you could hand a 4-year-old with 620 Pokemon. Nothing is removed; it is a lens, not a filter that hides.

title: The versus button calls the other brother "P 2"
body:
On Gabe's GYM CIRCUIT the shared-play bar reads "VS  GABE  VS  P 2". On Art's it reads "VS  ART  VS  P 2". Same button, same anonymous second seat, whichever brother is holding the phone.

The game knows both boys' names everywhere else — the chip in the top-left says GABE or ART, the box header says GABE'S PC BOX and ART'S PC BOX. The one screen that exists because there are two children is the screen that drops a name. And the second half is styled fainter than the first: GABE is white on red, P 2 is grey-blue on blue. The younger seat is literally lower contrast.

Both halves are words, so Art has nothing at all here. He cannot read ART, he cannot read P 2, and the red-and-blue bar gives him no clue which end is him.

In these runs player 2 was never named — which is the state every family is in on day one, before anyone thinks to open Settings. That is exactly the moment the second child matters. Put each boy's lead Pokémon sprite on his half of the bar and the button works before anyone types anything.

title: Art's quest reward is Gabe's quest reward, word for word
body:
I put the Junior shot and the normal shot next to each other and they are the same panel, pixel for pixel: a star, "QUEST COMPLETE!", "Catch a GRASS type — done!", "+30 XP to your lead Pokémon!", and a button that says AWESOME!. Sentence case, lowercase words, an accented é, four lines of prose.

Junior Mode rewrites the dex, the battle move buttons and the PC box for Art. It does not touch the one panel that hands out rewards.

What that costs is bigger than one modal. Gabe can read "catch a Grass type", decide to go and do it, and come back for the star. Art can only be surprised by stars. The entire quest system is a game his brother plays deliberately and he receives by accident. Nothing is taken from him — he gets the XP either way — but he never gets to aim, and aiming is the fun part.

Say it as pictures: the Grass type tile he needs, then the same tile with a tick. He already reads type colour fine elsewhere.

(Both shots are filenamed STILL-OPEN — a second modal was queued behind the first.)

title: Art tapped BACK three times and stayed in the fight
body:
A wild Gligar appears in Art's battle. There is a BACK arrow in the top-left corner, exactly where it should be. He taps it three times. The screen does not change — same Gligar, same Charizard, same "WILD GLIGAR APPEARED!", not a flicker of feedback on the chip itself. The field is idle; nothing is animating that a tap could be waiting on.

Then the harness held the chip down for a second and it worked. Out to the dex.

Press-and-hold is a gesture a four-year-old does not invent. He taps. When tapping the one obvious exit does nothing three times in a row, the honest conclusion for a small child is that the game is broken, or that he is stuck in the fight — and "I want to stop now" is a thing he can't say to a screen that won't take a tap.

Gabe survives this because he'll win the battle out instead, or discover the hold. One escape hatch, tuned for the brother who can already read.

If the hold is deliberate, show it: fill the arrow as he presses, so holding is something he can discover by accident. (May share a root cause with F-044.)
rule_risk: Junior Mode never punishes — being unable to leave a fight on a tap is the closest thing to being trapped

title: The whole app changes hands when the name chip does
body:
Same phone, same Pokémon — #0026 RAICHU — two brothers, and they are not looking at the same program.

Gabe's screen: a search field between the arrows, a DATA button, a red CATCH. Art's screen: no search box at all, no DATA, the arrows grown into two fat halves of a row, and a green OWNED tile with a big tick where CATCH used to be. Junior Mode isn't a flag bolted onto a shared layout, it's a different app, and it follows whichever name is in the top-left chip.

And the part I'd protect hardest: nothing on Art's screen says junior, easy, little, helper, or mode. He gets a simpler Pokédex and no explanation of why he got it. That's the rule kept perfectly, and it's the kind of thing that quietly dies in a refactor when someone adds a helpful "JUNIOR MODE ON" banner.

So make this the regression test, twice over: assert the junior dex renders no search input and no DATA button, and assert no string matching /junior|easy|kid|helper/i ever appears in the DOM on a junior screen. Red build if either leaks.

title: Let Gabe give Art a Pokémon
body:
Two boxes, one device, one house. GABE'S PC BOX: six generation tabs, 151, 100/100, 135/135, 107/107, 127/156, 620-something, and page one is nothing but Lv55 shinies. ART'S PC BOX: three caught on the first page, everything after it a black silhouette, and six empty dotted holes along the top.

There is no door between those two collections. They're brothers.

I'd like a GIFT button on a Pokémon in the PC box. Gabe picks one, taps the other name chip, and it lands in Art's box wearing a small ribbon — and the ribbon is a sprite of Gabe's lead Pokémon, not the word "from". Art needs no reading for that: a new one appeared, it has a ribbon, someone gave it to him.

Nothing leaves Gabe's box unless he chooses it, and it should refuse to hand over his last copy of anything, so nobody's collection ever shrinks by surprise.

The reason I want this isn't the Pokémon. Right now the only thing a 620-strong collection lets the older brother do is be further ahead. This gives him something to do with it that makes the little one happier.

title: A full tablet leaves a Pokémon caught but unrecorded
body:
I loaded Gabe's 620-Pokémon save, filled the tablet's storage to the brim, then caught Bisharp with a Master Ball. The game said GOTCHA!, spent the ball (9 to 8) and counted the catch (620 to 621). Then I reloaded, the way Gabe would on Saturday. The dex says 621/649. But there is no record for Bisharp at all — only the tick that he exists. He comes back as Lv5, alone in a box where every other Pokémon is Lv55.

One catch writes the save several times: the tick, the level, the ball count. When room runs out, some of those writes land and some don't, so what ends up on disk is a save the game itself could never have produced. In a harsher run the whole catch vanished and the Master Ball was still gone — a ball spent on nothing.

Gabe's 620 Pokémon are 21 KB, four-tenths of one percent of what the tablet allows this game. It isn't his collection filling the disk (see my other thread), and it shouldn't be his collection that pays.
rule_risk: saves are sacred
never take something away from a child

title: The Pokédex cache quietly grows until it fills the tablet
body:
I watched the storage while I browsed. At boot the game holds 21 KB of Gabe's collection and 10 KB of cached Pokémon data. After paging through 200 species the cached data was 1.8 million characters — about 8.7 KB per Pokémon, growing in a straight line with no ceiling I could find. The whole dex is 649 species. That projects to roughly 5.7 MB against a budget of about 5.2 MB.

So the hoarder save in my slice — 620 caught, 96% of the dex, exactly the boy who looks at everything — is on a path to fill the tablet by playing normally. And the collection is not what fills it: Gabe's 620 Pokémon are 21 KB. The cache is 85 times bigger than the thing it endangers.

When the wall is hit the game throws the entire cache away to protect the save (good, and I've praised it separately), then refetches everything from scratch — slow sprites and blank data sheets at Grandma's house on bad wifi, then it fills up and does it again.

A cap — newest 150 species, say — would end this.

title: The out-of-storage warning can't reach either boy
body:
When the save fails, the game does the right thing and stops everything: a full red screen that will not go away when you tap it. I'm glad it exists. But look at what it says: a warning triangle, SHOW A GROWN-UP, and then twenty-six words of prose — "This tablet is out of storage, so the game cannot save. Please stop playing and tell Dad now, before anything is lost."

Art cannot read one word of that. To him it is a red screen that ate his game, and the only thing he can do is close the app — which is exactly how the message never reaches you. Gabe can decode it, slowly, in a plain system font this game uses nowhere else.

This is the single most important screen in the app: it is the moment his collection is at stake, and it is the one screen written entirely in words. Give it a picture a four-year-old acts on (a red full-up tablet, a Poké Ball that won't close) and one big button that goes straight to COPY CODE / SAVE FILE, so whoever is holding the tablet can rescue the save on the spot.

title: The import path is the safest thing in this codebase
body:
I tried to destroy Gabe's 620-Pokémon save through the settings screen and could not.

A junk code is refused with "NOT LOADED — That save code was not recognized. Nothing was changed." A real code is gated behind the grown-up PIN, and before it takes effect it counts the cost out loud: "Before: 621 Pokémon. Now: 2 Pokémon. That code has FEWER Pokémon than you had. If this is wrong, tap UNDO IMPORT right now to put it back." It names the exact button. Behind the scenes the old save is kept whole in a second key. UNDO IMPORT then asks the PIN again, confirms, and hands all 620 back exactly — and the save it displaced becomes the new undo, so the swap runs both ways and nothing is ever destroyed. Export offers both a downloadable file and a clipboard code, with a select-it-yourself fallback if the clipboard is blocked.

That is proper data engineering: read is free, write is guarded, every destructive step is reversible and says what it costs first. Please keep a test on the before/after counts and on the two-way undo.

title: Back the boys up on a schedule, not on my memory
body:
The game already knows how to keep a spare copy — it makes one every time somebody imports, and that copy is what UNDO IMPORT restores. It only ever does it when a grown-up is standing at the settings screen. Every other day of the year there is exactly one copy of both boys' collections, in one browser key, on one tablet.

Two small things, no schema change and no new screens:

First, on the first boot of each day, copy the save into a second dated key before anything else writes. Twenty-one kilobytes. If a write ever lands half-finished, yesterday's whole collection is still sitting there.

Second, put one line under SAVE DATA: LAST COPY — 23 DAYS AGO, in red once it passes a fortnight. I have no way of knowing right now whether the last file you saved was August or February, and neither do you. A number is enough to make you tap SAVE FILE on the way to bed.

A rebuilt Pokédex is a weekend. Six hundred and twenty Pokémon is two years of Saturdays.

title: The service worker never installs. There is no offline.
body:
I played a normal wifi session, then cleared only the ordinary browser cache — what an iPhone does on its own after a few days in a pocket — and pulled the network. The app came up as a white screen. No boot logo, no TAP TO START, nothing: net::ERR_INTERNET_DISCONNECTED.

The reason is one line. sw.js lists ./js/fx.js twice in SHELL_FILES, and the browser refuses a cache list containing a duplicate: "InvalidStateError: Failed to execute 'addAll' on 'Cache': Cache.addAll(): duplicate requests (.../js/fx.js)". The install rejects, the registration is discarded, and the cache it opened sits there with 0 files in it. Six runs out of six, on two different servers.

So nothing in sw.js has ever run on the boys' tablet: no cached shell, and no sprite cache either — every sprite, animation and cry is re-downloaded on every single launch, which is exactly the bandwidth fix the comment in that file celebrates.

I copied the app, deleted the duplicate line, and re-ran the same test: 27 shell files cached, 18 sprites, and the game opened and played with the network off.

title: One bad second of wifi breaks a sprite forever
body:
This one only bites after the service worker is fixed, so please read it alongside the install bug rather than instead of it.

Sprites are cache-first, and the cache write accepts opaque responses. Opaque means the browser will not tell you whether it was a picture or a 404 — status is 0 either way. I asked the working build for a sprite that does not exist; the failure went straight into pokedexos-assets as a stored response. Then I put the network back to perfect and relaunched: Pikachu is a grey Poké Ball on the dex, and stays one.

Nothing ever repairs it. That cache is deliberately version-independent — a good decision for bandwidth — so a release bump will not clear it, and nothing prunes it. The only cure is clearing site data on the tablet, which is also where the saves live.

One flaky minute on hotel wifi, and whichever Pokémon the boys happened to be looking at is a blank ball on their dex until someone does surgery. A caught Pokémon losing its picture permanently is a thing being taken away.
rule_risk: Never take something away from a child: a Pokemon they caught can permanently lose its picture, with no way back inside the game.

title: The pixel font comes from Google, so offline it's Courier
body:
Press Start 2P is the whole voice of this app, and it is the one asset that is not in the app. It is fetched from fonts.googleapis.com at boot and is not in the service worker's shell list — it only lands in the cache if it happens to be requested at a moment when the worker is already in charge, which on a first launch it is not.

So the first no-signal launch renders the entire game in the Courier fallback. Look at the shot: PIKACHU is a plain typeface, the level chip reads "Lv 1 4" with the digits pushed apart, the dex entry reads "0 . 4 m", the toolbar labels lose their weight. It is legible, and it does not fall off the screen at 390 — but it is a different app, and it is the one the boys would meet in the car.

The font file is about 10KB. Putting the woff2 in the repo, serving it from a local @font-face, and adding it to the shell list removes Google from the boot path entirely — also worth having on any wifi that blocks Google Fonts.

title: With no signal, the game never once scolds them
body:
I cut the network mid-session and kept playing: the dex, the explore list, the gym circuit, the ball drawer. Not one error box, not one banner, not the word "offline" anywhere. Sandslash's page still had its type tile, its height, its weight and its genus, because the API data lives in a local projection rather than being re-fetched. The habitat list is entirely local and looked identical to the online run.

And when a picture genuinely cannot arrive, what appears is a hand-drawn Poké Ball — an inline SVG, so the fallback itself can never fail to load. It is the right size, it sits in the same glow, and it looks deliberate. Compare that to the grey broken-image icon that is the web's default answer, which would read to Art as "you broke it".

That is the whole degradation philosophy done right: the picture and colour keep working, and a four-year-old cannot tell that anything went wrong. Please keep this. If a future change ever swaps that ball for a browser broken-image glyph, or adds a "YOU ARE OFFLINE" modal, it should fail the suite.

title: Pack my own Pokemon for the car
body:
Once the worker installs, the shell is safe but the pictures still are not: sprites only cache after they have been looked at, and even the four balls in the drawer are remote PNGs. Offline in the car, a boy scrolling to a Pokemon he has never opened gets a blank ball, and if the drawer was never opened on wifi it is four blank balls.

What I would like, on wifi and quietly in the background: warm the cache with the things that are certainly theirs — the six on the team, the four ball icons, and the sprites for everything already caught, oldest first, a few at a time so it never competes with the game. Nothing new appears on screen; the car ride just works.

And one thing for Kevin: a tiny Poké Ball on the boot screen, filled when the app is fully packed and hollow when it is not. No words, no percentage. It would have told you in one glance that sw.js has never once installed, which is the bug that took me a day to find.

title: Green BACK bar parks on top of Art's Pokemon
body:
I measured the pixels in E-0037. Art's PC grid scrolls under a fixed, full-width green BACK bar. The fourth row of Pokemon ends cleanly, then row five appears — and exactly 10 CSS pixels of it are visible before the green bar covers the rest.

That 10px sliver is the problem. A four-year-old reaching for a partly-visible thing does not aim at the sliver; he plants his whole fingertip (8-10mm, roughly 20-25 CSS px on this phone) at the top of what he can see. The centre of that contact patch lands on BACK. So the reach that means "show me the next one" performs "leave the box" instead.

This is the worst mis-tap trade in his whole session: the biggest, brightest target on the screen (a 335x63 CSS slab) is the destructive one, and it is physically overlapping the content he wants. E-0023 shows the same overlap on a fresh save.

Give the scroll area bottom padding equal to the bar's height so the last row can clear it, or float BACK as a corner button instead of a full-width slab.

title: The two rows Art must aim at have 5px gaps
body:
Everywhere else this app spaces things beautifully. I measured: habitat cards 18 CSS px apart (E-0040), battle move tiles 11 px apart (E-0041). Then the two rows Art actually has to aim at drop to 5 px.

Ball drawer (E-0043): four ball rows, each 65 CSS px tall, separated by 5 px. Then MASTER BALL to CANCEL is 14 px — nearly three times the separation, and CANCEL is the only saturated red on a cream sheet, so it is also the thing his eye goes to first. The gaps are backwards. The choices are crowded together and the exit gets the elbow room.

PC gen tabs (E-0037): six tabs, 56 x 52 CSS px, 5.5 px apart, and four of the six are told apart only by a 20 px green starter sprite. At 5 px separation with 20 px discriminators, a mis-tap is near-certain — and the entire box silently swaps contents with no transition, so his Pokemon just vanish.

For a four-year-old I would want 12 px minimum between adjacent targets. The app already does 11-18 px elsewhere; these two rows just need to match.

title: The card's two controls are the smallest targets in Junior
body:
Adding measurements to this thread rather than opening a second one, because the missing close button is only half of what is wrong here.

In E-0038 the tapped-Pokemon card has exactly two controls. The favourite star is about 45 CSS px and drawn as a half-disc straddling the card's top-right corner, so part of its visual mass sits over the dimmed backdrop rather than the card. The play/cry button is an orange glyph roughly 25 x 24 CSS px, sitting inside a much larger empty bordered row — if only the glyph is live, that is the smallest target in Art's entire session by a wide margin.

So the one screen with no exit is also the screen with the two hardest things to hit. A four-year-old's aimed tap has roughly a 10 mm error radius; a 25 px target is inside the noise. He will tap the cream space around it repeatedly, get nothing, and start mashing — which is how the blank-screen reports elsewhere in this forum begin.

If the whole bordered row is already tappable, say so visually: fill it, do not outline it.

title: The explore map is motor-perfect and should be the template
body:
E-0040 is the best-designed screen for a four-year-old's hands in this whole review, and I want it locked down so nobody optimises it away.

Measured: each habitat is a single full-width card, roughly 340 x 115 CSS px, stacked with 18 CSS px of dead space between them. That is about 30 mm of target with 3 mm of separation. There is no aiming involved — Art puts his hand somewhere on the screen and he has chosen a place. I could not make him mis-tap this if I tried.

It also earns its size. Each card carries a big habitat icon, three example Pokemon sprites, and a gold ring around the currently-selected one. A pre-reader gets the picture, the inhabitants and the state without a single word doing load-bearing work.

Every other Junior screen should be measured against this one. Regression test worth keeping: no habitat card narrower than the content column, no vertical gap under 16 CSS px, and the selected card keeps a visible ring rather than only a colour shift.

title: Let Junior Mode's hit areas be bigger than its boxes
body:
The fixes for most of what I filed are the same one fix, and it does not require redrawing anything.

In Junior Mode, give every interactive element an invisible hit area larger than its painted box: a floor of 60 x 60 CSS px, and at least 12 CSS px of genuinely dead space between neighbouring hit areas. The art stays exactly as Kevin drew it. Only the catchment grows.

That single rule would fix the 5 px ball rows (E-0043), the 5.5 px gen tabs, and the 25 px play glyph (E-0038) without touching a single sprite or breaking a layout. In a zero-build vanilla app it is a handful of CSS on the junior selectors — padding plus a negative margin, or a generous pseudo-element overlay.

Why 60 rather than the usual 44: 44 px comes from adult guidance. A four-year-old's aimed tap scatters roughly twice as far, and Art is often aiming one-handed while the other hand holds the phone. 44 px is the floor for Gabe. It is the ceiling of what fails for Art.

And it costs Gabe nothing — his mode is untouched.

title: A seven-year-old can set the PIN and lock me out
body:
I held PARENT TOOLS on a fresh device and got "GROWN-UPS ONLY — SET A NEW PIN" (20-mouse-hold-still-1600ms.png). It never asked who I was. Whoever holds that button first owns the gate, and Gabe reads well enough to find it.

That would be survivable if the PIN only guarded Parent Tools. It doesn't. One tap on PASTE CODE lands on the same pad (10-paste-code-one-tap.png), and LOAD FILE and UNDO IMPORT sit behind it too. So the person who sets the PIN owns the entire restore path for both boys' saves.

I went looking for a way back and the only one that exists is in the v18.8.0 changelog: open the game on a computer, press F12, type a localStorage command. The save lives on their iPad. There is no F12 on an iPad, the PIN is per-device, and clearing website data to reset it would take the save with it.

So the worst Sunday morning is: Gabe set a PIN in March, I need to restore in September, and my only options are a command line the device doesn't have or wiping 202 Pokémon.
rule_risk: Saves are sacred — the only in-app route back to a lost save can be claimed by a child, with no parent recovery on the device that holds it
seat: KEVIN'S OWN SEAT — the dad, not a developer

title: SAVE FILE says nothing at all, either way
body:
I tapped 📄 SAVE FILE and took a shot immediately after (31-after-save-file-tap.png). The screen is byte-identical to the shot I took before the tap (30-before-save-file.png). No dialog, no filename, no tick. The download did fire underneath — I caught it in the harness, pokedex-save-2026-09-02.json — but nothing on screen says so.

Compare COPY CODE right next to it: one tap and I get a card with a floppy disk on it telling me exactly what happened (32-after-copy-code-tap.png). Same row of buttons, opposite behaviour.

This is the button that exists so I can back up 202 Pokémon and 58 gym wins (E-0098, E-0070). It's the only one I'd press on a Sunday morning before touching anything, and it gives me nothing to believe. On the boys' installed iPad, a blob download from a home-screen PWA is exactly the thing that quietly does nothing — and if it did nothing, this screen would look identical to the screen I'm looking at now.

I'd rather it lied loudly than succeeded in silence. Tell me the filename, or tell me it failed.
seat: KEVIN'S OWN SEAT — the dad, not a developer

title: The version number is 1.57 to 1 on the splash
body:
After every push, the one thing I do is open the game on their iPad and check the version, because a stale cached shell looks exactly like a working one.

On the boot splash the version is 8px cream on olive green. I sampled the pixels out of the screenshot: text (203,205,135) on background (139,172,15). That is 1.57 to 1. Four and a half is the floor for readable text. At arm's length on a bright kitchen table I genuinely cannot tell 19.8.0 from 18.8.0 (02-settings-bottom.png).

In Settings it's better but still 8px, colour rgb(112,104,72), the smallest text on the page and the smallest the project allows — and it's filed under the heading SOUND, sitting between MUSIC & SOUND and BUZZ (30-before-save-file.png). The version of the game is not a sound setting.

This is the cheapest fix in my whole list. Make the splash version readable, and move the Settings row up under its own heading with the boys' data. It costs nothing and it's the only diagnostic a non-developer has.
seat: KEVIN'S OWN SEAT — the dad, not a developer

title: One tap on PASTE CODE lands on the PIN pad
body:
I went at the save block expecting to find it wide open, because that's where I'd have left a hole. It isn't.

I tapped 📋 PASTE CODE once, straight from the gear icon, with no hold and no ceremony. I did not get a paste box. I got 🔒 GROWN-UPS ONLY (10-paste-code-one-tap.png). The three buttons that can replace both boys' collections — PASTE CODE, LOAD FILE, UNDO IMPORT — are all behind the same gate, and they're grouped under a heading that says out loud SAVE DATA (BOTH PLAYERS) so I know the blast radius before I touch anything (30-before-save-file.png).

And the fence has a second half: ↩️ UNDO IMPORT sits right there in the same block, so a bad paste is a mistake instead of a catastrophe.

This is the thing I would most hate to see quietly regress in some future tidy-up of the Settings screen. Please put a test on it: tapping set-import-paste, set-import-file or set-undo-import with no PIN stored must land on the keypad, and UNDO IMPORT must never leave that block.
seat: KEVIN'S OWN SEAT — the dad, not a developer

title: Tell me when this save was last backed up
body:
Look at what's actually in there now: 202 Pokémon, all twelve stops beaten, 58 out of 58 trainers, a Hall of Fame team (E-0098, E-0070, E-0072). Gabe built that over months. There is no version of losing it that is a bug report — it's a bad evening in our house.

And nowhere on this screen does the game tell me whether any of it has ever left the iPad (30-before-save-file.png). Five buttons, no dates. I have to remember, and I won't.

What I want is small and boring:

A line under SAVE DATA that reads LAST BACKED UP — 12 AUG, or NEVER in red. That alone would make me press the button.

And a snapshot the game takes for itself — one automatic dated copy a week, kept alongside the live save, restorable from Parent Tools without me having thought ahead. UNDO IMPORT already proves you can hold a second save shape safely; this is the same trick pointed at time instead of at imports.

I'd rather the game remembered than trust me to.
seat: KEVIN'S OWN SEAT — the dad, not a developer

title: The dex cache grows forever inside the save's 5 MB
body:
I booted Gabe's hoarder save (620 caught, E-0110) and did nothing but press NEXT while watching localStorage. The API cache starts at 10 KB and grows about 9 KB per Pokemon, with no ceiling and no eviction: 219 KB after 25 taps, 921 KB after 100, 2,695 KB after 300. localStorage is one 5,120 KB box per site (I measured the wall), and the save lives in that same box - 21 KB at 620 caught. On this trajectory the cache alone reaches the wall around 550 Pokemon browsed, and the boy closest to that is the one with the most to lose.

I then filled storage to the brim and asked for a save write: QuotaExceededError. The good news is the previous save stayed intact and parseable, and the game did not crash. The bad news is that nothing anywhere says a write failed - the dex sat there showing Clefairy as if the session was being recorded (quota-brim.png).

A cap of a few hundred cache entries, oldest out, would keep the save's room free forever.
rule_risk: saves are sacred: the uncapped API cache and the save share one 5 MB localStorage box, and a save write at the ceiling fails silently

title: Every NEXT tap is a full network round trip
body:
On my laptop's connection each NEXT settles in about 200 ms and everything is fine (E-0113 to E-0117 look instant). I re-ran the same taps on a throttled phone profile - slow 4G, 4x CPU - and each NEXT took 700 to 1,450 ms.

What that second looks like matters. At +250 ms after one tap, the bottom two thirds of the dex is gone: no sprite, no arrows, no search box, no CRY or EXPLORE or GYMS, just flat navy under the header (next-plus250ms-4g.png). After six quick taps I was on NIDORINA with a name, a type and an empty spotlight, sprite still not decoded (mash-6-taps-4g.png). This is the same emptiness F-012 and F-021 report in Junior Mode, and it is not a Junior bug - it is the network, in normal mode, at 390x844.

The cost per Pokemon is 57 KB: a 30 KB animated GIF (Raichu's is 66 KB) plus two or three chained API calls. Twenty taps pulled 1.14 MB. Nothing is fetched before it is needed.

title: Those 404s are cries, and they download with sound off
body:
Replying rather than re-filing: I ran the hoarder save against the real cry CDN to see what the machine's 404 reports actually cost, and found something sitting next to them.

Every dex entry fetches its cry .ogg the moment the Pokemon appears - before anyone presses CRY, and while the app is muted. I set pokedexos_muted=1 (the top bar shows the red no-sound sign in every shot in my slice, E-0113), booted, pressed NEXT five times, and six .ogg files went out. Over twenty Pokemon that is 237 KB of audio, about 12 KB each, for sound that is switched off. On the boys' iPhones it is worse than wasted: Safari cannot decode Ogg at all, so those bytes can never make a noise under any setting.

That is roughly a fifth of the 1.14 MB a twenty-Pokemon browse costs, spent on silence. Fetching the cry only when CRY is pressed, and not at all while muted, costs the boys nothing they can hear.

No product rule is broken here - nothing talks, and the chiptune fallback is doing its job.

title: The 620-Pokemon box is genuinely cheap to open
body:
I came to this seat expecting the PC box to be the thing that falls over, because 620 caught is where a phone usually gives up. It doesn't.

Opening the box on Gabe's hoarder save (E-0110, E-0137) builds a 151-card Gen 1 grid; tapping ALL builds all 649 cards, 3,707 DOM nodes. With the CPU throttled 4x, that ALL tap blocked the main thread for 32 ms - under two frames. Every one of the 649 images carries loading="lazy", so only about 120 sprites are actually requested; scrolling to Genesect at the bottom of a 21,110 px grid pulls the rest in as they arrive, and the bottom row renders complete (pc-all-bottom-4x.png). I opened and closed the box three times: node count stayed at 3,708 every time, no growth, no leak, and reopening is instant because the grid is kept.

Worth pinning as a regression test: assert every card image in the PC grid has loading="lazy", and that DOM node count is unchanged across three open/close cycles on a 600+ save. Both would catch the day someone drops the lazy attribute.

title: Fetch the next Pokemon before he asks for it
body:
While Gabe is looking at #025, the game already knows the two entries he might ask for next: #024 and #026. It could quietly fetch them - the JSON, the sprite, nothing else - during the seconds he spends looking. Then NEXT paints instantly instead of costing the 700 to 1,450 ms I measured on a phone-shaped connection, and the bottom half of the dex never has to disappear while it waits (next-plus250ms-4g.png).

This costs no extra data on average: he was going to fetch those bytes anyway, one tap later. It just moves the fetch into time he is already standing still. Two entries deep is enough; the cache the app already keeps does the rest, and it is very good at its job - a second pass over the same 30 Pokemon dropped from 73 API calls to 5.

The version of this I would love most: pre-warm the neighbours the moment an entry settles, and show the still PNG (600 bytes, already downloaded) in the spotlight until the 30 KB animated one arrives. Nobody would ever see an empty stage again.

title: ERROR / TIMEOUT is the biggest word on Art's screen
body:
Nobody had taken this shot, so I took it: I left the wifi working and killed the route out to pokeapi.co and the sprite host — a hotel, a school guest network, a car park, grandma's house. That is what the game does the moment the internet blinks.

Art's dex fills the whole top of the screen with ERROR / TIMEOUT in the largest letters the app owns, then a torn-page broken-image glyph where his Pokemon should be, then # - - -. He cannot read one of those twelve letters. What he can read is that the picture broke and the game is shouting about it. Gabe can read it, and will conclude he broke something.

CATCH stays big and red underneath. EXPLORE and GYMS stay lit. Nothing says "this is the wifi, not you," and nothing walks him to his PC box or trainer card, which are on the phone and still work fine.

The app is honest with a developer and frightening to a four-year-old. It needs a picture-only sleeping-Poke-Ball face and a nudge toward the parts that still work.
rule_risk: Junior Mode never punishes: the loudest thing on Art's screen is a failure message, for something that was not his fault
Never take something away from a child: one dropped connection removes all 649 Pokemon and replaces them with the word ERROR

title: SPARKLE is the one badge you cannot work for
body:
On the champion card, next to CURATOR (202/300) and PROFESSOR (202/649), sits SPARKLE: "Catch your first shiny — 0/1". Scroll down and STATS confirms it: SHINIES 0, after 202 catches and 58 battles won.

Every other locked badge on that card is a promise the boys can keep by playing. Do the work, the fraction moves. SPARKLE's fraction has never moved and cannot be made to move — it is a dice roll wearing a progress counter. And the dex has a SHINY button that shows Gabe the sparkly version of anything he likes, whenever he likes, so he knows exactly what he is not getting.

That is a slot machine dressed as an achievement, aimed at a seven-year-old. It is the one place in this very generous game where the honest answer to "how do I get that one, Dad?" is "you don't, you just keep going."

Either give it a floor — after N catches with no shiny, the next one sparkles — or drop the 0/1 and let it be a surprise instead of a scoreboard.

title: Today's Quests is the only number that goes backwards
body:
Scrolled to the middle of the champion trainer card: CAUGHT 202. BATTLES WON 58. BADGES 14/18. TOP LEVEL 62. Every one of those only ever climbs.

Directly above them: TODAY'S QUESTS — Win a battle 0/1, Catch a ROCK type 0/1, Catch a WATER type 0/1, Evolve 2 Pokemon 0/2. Four empty checkboxes on the save of a boy who has beaten all 58 trainers.

Those four boxes were ticked yesterday. At midnight they emptied, and nothing anywhere records that they were ever full. This isn't a streak, so it doesn't break the rule outright — but it is the same shape, and it is the one board in the game that erases a child's work on a timer he can't see. A four-year-old who filled it in on Saturday and opens the app on Sunday morning has simply been told he didn't.

Cheapest fix that costs nothing and breaks nothing: a QUESTS DONE all-time counter in STATS, so the ticks go somewhere permanent when the day rolls over.
rule_risk: Never take something away from a child: yesterday's four completed quests are deleted overnight with no permanent record

title: Art's ball drawer keeps the secret perfectly
body:
Put the two drawers side by side and this is the best-kept promise in the app.

Gabe's drawer: "Weaker Pokemon are easier to catch!" at the top, BETTER WHEN WEAKENED under three balls, and MASTER BALL x 5 — NEVER FAILS. The full truth, including the fact that the good one runs out.

Art's drawer: THROW A BALL. Four balls. Four names. No subtitle, no odds, no counts, no NEVER FAILS, no x 5.

It does not tell him his balls always work. It does not tell him they might not. It does not put a cheerful little ALWAYS WORKS! badge on anything. He picks the purple one because it's purple, it works, and he feels like he chose well — which is exactly what rule 2 asks for and is genuinely hard to get right.

Please make this a regression test. The instinct to "be helpful" and add a caption or a count to Art's drawer will come back, and the day it does, the accommodation starts advertising itself.

title: A wind-down that never takes anything away
body:
I walked a full simulated Saturday: three catches, a wild fight, a gym, the PC box, one more gym fight. Thirty-three screens. Not one of them is a resting place.

The victory modal's only button is CONTINUE. The dex's two biggest, brightest buttons are EXPLORE and GYMS. The end of the session is a wall of green REMATCH bars. Every exit in this game is a door further in, and BACK is the only way out — a word Art can't read.

So, a wish, and please build it as the opposite of a lockout. After a length Kevin sets in Parent Tools, nothing is removed and nothing is refused: the game just gets sleepy. Green fades to dusk, EXPLORE and GYMS go quiet, and the PC box opens by itself on today's catches with their cries — a goodnight card made of the sprites he earned, not a sentence.

Worth saying: the trainer card counts catches, badges, levels and wins, and not one minute of clock. The app keeps no timer on your children. Keep it that way — put the clock in Kevin's hands, not in the save.
